about: Broad Street Station in 1943 and the lines out of Richmond: the railroad map framed by fourteen places. Made with tools/sets/set.py; see 'Making a set' in the README.
title: Broad Street Station, 1943
subtitle: Richmond's union station at its wartime height, and the railroads that ran from it
note: Track is today's, dated by the era rules, with the station loop traced from the USGS quadrangles of 1934 and 1956; the station is modeled from its plans, postcards and the 1925 Sanborn sheets, its heights approximate. Buildings are today's that stood by 1943, by the city's recorded year built, with lost ones traced from the 1925 Sanborn sheets, their outlines and heights approximate. Trains are illustrative.
credit: isoscape by Chris Busse  ·  Map data © OpenStreetMap contributors (ODbL)  ·  Elevation: USGS 3DEP  ·  Buildings dated from City of Richmond assessor records and traced from Sanborn maps (Library of Congress)  ·  Station loop after the USGS Richmond quadrangles of 1934 and 1956
ground_note: The ground is today’s, from lidar: cuts and fills made since (the interstates, the Downtown Expressway, the floodwall) show in it.

boxes.title: AY Tower
boxes.subtitle: Where the Coast Line met the RF&P
boxes.note: About a mile northwest of the station, the RF&P main line from Washington met the Atlantic Coast Line's Belt Line at the wye called AY, its switches worked from AY Tower (not drawn: no source here places it). Trains for the Coast Line swung south onto the Belt Line here; Broad Street trains took the third leg down to the station.

boxes.title: The State Fair grounds
boxes.subtitle: North Boulevard, 1940
boxes.note: From 1906 the State Fair filled these grounds north of the tracks every fall, around its racetrack. Parker Field went up on them in 1934 (not drawn here), a ballpark only from 1954. The fair association bought Strawberry Hill in 1941 and held its first fair there after the war, in 1946. The Diamond stands on the site.

boxes.title: Scott's Addition
boxes.subtitle: Warehouses between the RF&P and the Belt Line
boxes.note: Laid out for houses west of the Boulevard, Scott's Addition was zoned for industry in 1927, and spurs from the railroads ran into its streets. By 1943 the National Biscuit Company, here since 1923, had General Baking's new plant, two dairies and a bag factory for neighbors. The warehouses now hold breweries, cideries and apartments.

boxes.title: Seaboard Junction
boxes.subtitle: Where the Seaboard left the RF&P
boxes.note: Just north of the station the Seaboard Air Line's main line left the RF&P and ran southeast to Main Street Station. Seaboard trains between Washington and the South passed Broad Street by; only from 1959 did they call there, backing in. The Seaboard and the Coast Line merged in 1967.

boxes.title: The loop and the sheds
boxes.subtitle: Nine tracks under butterfly sheds
boxes.note: Trains ran in off the RF&P at one end of the loop and out at the other. Seven passenger tracks and two express tracks lay along 1,200 feet of cast-iron butterfly sheds, with ramps up to the concourse. In 1943 the station averaged 57 trains a day; on April 22 it handled a record 33,324 passengers.

boxes.title: C.F. Sauer Company
boxes.subtitle: Broad Street at Hermitage Road
boxes.note: The extract house Conrad Sauer founded at 17th and Broad in 1887 moved to Broad and Hermitage in 1911, by the rail sidings. When Sauer died in 1927 it was the country's largest producer of extracts and spices. The headquarters is on the National Register, and the Sauer's Vanilla sign still lights Broad Street.

boxes.title: Main Street Station
boxes.subtitle: The Seaboard and the C&O
boxes.note: Downtown, the Seaboard Air Line and the C&O shared Main Street Station, opened in 1901: a head house under a steep hipped roof of red tile, its clock tower 110 feet to the finial, and behind it a gable-roofed train shed more than 500 feet long on the tracks' trestle, here in plain massing. The Seaboard moved to Broad Street in 1959; the C&O stayed until Amtrak took over in 1971.

boxes.title: The Triple Crossing
boxes.subtitle: Three railroads, three levels
boxes.note: Just east of 14th and Dock streets the C&O's viaduct crossed over the Seaboard, which crossed over the Southern on the ground: three railroads at three levels, built in 1900 and 1901. Now and then the railroads staged photographs with a train on every level. CSX and Norfolk Southern trains still cross here.

boxes.title: The C&O viaduct
boxes.subtitle: Three miles along the river
boxes.note: In 1901 the C&O raised its line on a viaduct along the north bank of the James, three miles of trestle past Tredegar and down Dock Street, so trains of coal for Newport News bypassed the crowded route through the city. CSX coal trains still run on it.

boxes.title: Hull Street Station
boxes.subtitle: The Southern in Manchester
boxes.note: Across the river, the Southern Railway's trains for Danville left from Hull Street Station, built in 1915 when the Southern gave up its passenger depot on 14th Street. Passenger service ended in 1957. The station reopened in 2011 as the Richmond Railroad Museum.

boxes.title: The Belt Line bridge
boxes.subtitle: The Coast Line over the James
boxes.note: Coast Line trains for Petersburg and Florida crossed the James on the Belt Line's double-track bridge, opened with Broad Street Station in 1919, drawn here as a deck on piers. It carries CSX trains today.

boxes.title: Hotel William Byrd
boxes.subtitle: Across Broad from the station
boxes.note: Built in 1925 for the passengers across the street, the eleven-story William Byrd, designed by Marcellus Wright, had nearly 200 rooms; with the station it made the traveler's first picture of Richmond. It closed in the 1980s and has been apartments for older residents since 1996.

boxes.title: Broad Street Station
boxes.subtitle: From over the Fan
boxes.note: John Russell Pope set the station back from Broad Street on a built-up mound that screened the tracks behind it, facing the Fan's rowhouse blocks. The last train left on November 15, 1975; the Commonwealth bought the building, and the Science Museum of Virginia opened in it.

boxes.title: Pope's front
boxes.subtitle: Colonnade and dome
boxes.note: Opened January 6, 1919, the station was faced in Indiana limestone behind a colonnade after the Doric of St. Peter's Square, under the first dome on a major railroad station, its rotunda 100 feet high. In 1943 the dome was still tile; copper replaced it in 1955.

page.title: Broad Street Station, 1943
page.summary: Richmond's union station at its wartime peak, the loop of tracks it stood on, and fourteen places along the railroads that ran from it.
page.intro: John Russell Pope's Broad Street Station opened in January 1919 for the RF&P and the Atlantic Coast Line, and was never busier than in the Second World War: in 1943 it averaged 57 trains a day. This map draws Richmond's railroads as they ran that year, with the station's loop of tracks and its umbrella sheds, and frames it with fourteen places along the lines, from the wye at AY Tower to the Triple Crossing.
page.image_alt: The 1943 railroad map, framed by its fourteen places
page.how: The station is modeled from its 1919 plan, period postcards and the 1925 Sanborn fire-insurance sheet, its heights scaled from photographs and approximate. Its loop of tracks, long since taken up, is traced from the USGS Richmond quadrangles of 1934 and 1956 and fitted to the platforms that survive. The rest of the track is today's, as era rules date it. Buildings are those standing today that the city assessor dates to 1943 or before, with those traced from Sanborn maps around the station and downtown. On the big map the track is drawn four times its width; on the prints of single places, at its own.

menu.title: Broad Street Station, 1943: The Railroads and Fourteen Places
menu.blurb: Richmond's railroads as they ran in 1943, when Broad Street Station averaged 57 trains a day, drawn over the buildings then standing and framed by fourteen places along the lines, each with a short history: the station and its loop, the junctions, the depots downtown and across the river, and the bridges over the James.
